title: Guderian calls off Tula

facts.text: On the night of 4 December 1941 the temperature on the Moscow front fell to 25 below zero Fahrenheit. One German regiment on a night march had more than 300 frostbite cases, and several of its wounded froze to death.
Next morning tanks would not start, and machine guns and artillery would not fire because their lubricants and the oil in their recoil mechanisms had congealed.

General Heinz Guderian's Second Panzer Army had driven a deep bulge around the city of Tula, south of Moscow, which was held by the Soviet 50th Army and a regiment of Tula workers. On 2 December he began a hook to cut the city off.
On the morning of 5 December Guderian still thought he could take Tula. By evening his confidence had faded, and he proposed a gradual withdrawal from the whole bulge to the Don and Shat rivers.
His tanks, he complained, were breaking down in the cold while the Soviet tanks kept running. Field Marshal Fedor von Bock approved the withdrawal that night.
Tula never fell. Its defence, begun on 24 October, had lasted 43 days.
The retreat was costly too. Within two days one of his corps alone had 1,500 frostbite cases, 350 of them needing amputations, and many vehicles and guns had to be abandoned in the snow.

When Hitler's stand fast order arrived, Guderian told the army group's chief of staff he would file it and not pass it on, even under threat of a court martial. "I want at least to give my career a respectable ending."

He kept pulling back. On Christmas night his superior, Field Marshal Günther von Kluge, accused him of disobeying, and Guderian answered: "In these unusual circumstances I lead my army in a manner I can justify to my conscience."
The next morning an order arrived relieving Guderian of his command. Hitler, as an afterthought, forbade him to issue a farewell order to his troops. Some histories date the dismissal 25 December.
Guderian later told his side in his memoir Panzer Leader, which historians treat with care. In March 1943, after Stalingrad, Hitler brought him back as Inspector General of Armoured Troops.

photoNote: Tier: green. A panzer soldier salutes Generaloberst Heinz Guderian, who smiles and pats his arm, central sector of the Eastern Front, July 1941 (caption: Sowjetunion Mitte, Soldat vor Generaloberst Heinz Guderian salutierend; PK 689). Bundesarchiv Bild 101I-139-1112-17, photographer Ludwig Knobloch, CC BY-SA 3.0 de, via Wikimedia Commons. Saved 1920 x 1458 from the 1920 px thumbnail (original 3719 x 2824). Strong face, but it is summer and confident, five months before the card; the Knight's Cross and cap eagle are visible, so crop toward the face and do not frame it as admiring. The summer smile against the December failure can carry the contrast. Runner up: Guderian at a panzer regiment command post, August 1941, Bundesarchiv Bild 183-L19885, photographer Huschke, 800 x 524.

declassified.fact: Guderian wrote that he was given a Polish estate as a retirement gift. It was about 2,000 acres at Deipenhof in occupied Poland, its previous occupants had been evicted, and he had first asked for one three times larger.
